reasoning.Student A:
Because the mechanism guarantees that the set of schools I could possibly be matched with (my Obtainable Schools) is fixed given everyone else’s rankings and the schools’ priorities, my submitted ranking cannot change which schools are in that set. It only determines which school I receive among those obtainable — specifically, I will get the highest-ranked school from that fixed set.

Given that, the dominant (and risk-free) strategy is to list my true preferences. Doing so ensures that, whatever the Obtainable Schools turn out to be, I will receive the most-preferred school within that set. My priorities (w:1, y:1, x:2, z:2) and the fact that most other applicants favor y > x > w > z may affect which schools are in my Obtainable Schools, but they do not change the fact that my ranking cannot influence that set. Therefore I should rank honestly: w > y > x > z.
reasoning.Student B: Given the mechanism's key property, my submitted ranking cannot change which schools are in my Obtainable Schools set — it only determines which school I receive from that fixed set (I get the highest-ranked school among the obtainable ones). My true preference is w > x > y > z. Looking at priorities, I have top priority (1) at x and z and lower priority (2) at w and y; many other applicants favor y and x, so competition for y is likely high. Because my ranking cannot affect which schools are attainable for me, the dominant strategy is to rank sincerely: put my true most-preferred school first, then the next, etc., so that I receive the best school available to me. Therefore I submit my true preference order.
reasoning.Student C:
Because the set of schools I could possibly be matched with is fixed given others' rankings and priorities, my ranking cannot make new schools obtainable — it only picks the highest-ranked school within that fixed set.

Most other applicants favor y and x (y > x > w > z), and my priorities at y and z are low (4) while at w and x they are 3. Given that, I am unlikely to obtain y or x because many others who prefer y/x will beat me on priority. The realistic obtainable schools are therefore w and z. Since I prefer w over z, I should rank w first and z second. Placing y or x above w or z cannot make them obtainable, so it would only risk me getting a worse outcome within the obtainable set. Thus I submit my true preference order among all schools, with w first, then z, then y, then x.

Key property: my ranking cannot change which schools are in my Obtainable Schools; it only chooses which school I receive among that fixed set (I get my highest-ranked school among the obtainable ones).

Given my true preferences w > y > z > x, and the priority information (I am priority 4 at w and x, and 3 at y and z) and that most applicants favor y > x > w > z, the set of obtainable schools is determined by others' rankings and priorities and thus is fixed.

Because I cannot affect which schools are obtainable, the only relevant decision is to order schools within that set according to my true preferences so I receive the most-preferred obtainable school. Therefore I should list my sincere preference order: w first, then y, then z, then x.
